items.question: How is the R44 II described in the GENERAL paragraph of the Systems Description section?
options: Four-place, single main rotor, twin-engine helicopter with wheel-type landing gear
Four-place, single main rotor, single engine helicopter with skid-type landing gear
Two-place, coaxial rotor, single engine helicopter with skid-type landing gear
Four-place, single main rotor, single engine helicopter with retractable landing gear
items.explanation: Section 7 GENERAL states that the R44 II is a four-place, single main rotor, single engine helicopter constructed primarily of metal and equipped with skid-type landing gear.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: GENERAL (p.7-1)

items.question: What is the primary fuselage structure of the R44 II made of, according to Section 7?
options: Welded titanium tubing and composite skins
Cast aluminum frames and steel skins
Welded steel tubing and riveted aluminum sheet
Carbon fiber monocoque shell
items.explanation: The GENERAL paragraph explains that the primary fuselage structure is welded steel tubing and riveted aluminum sheet.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: GENERAL (p.7-1)

items.question: How is the tailcone of the R44 II constructed, and what carries most of the primary loads?
options: As a truss structure where internal frames carry most loads
As a monocoque structure where aluminum skins carry most primary loads
As a semi-monocoque structure with frames carrying all loads
As a tubular frame covered with fabric that carries primary loads
items.explanation: Section 7 states that the tailcone is a monocoque structure in which aluminum skins carry most primary loads.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: GENERAL (p.7-1)

items.question: Where are fiberglass and thermoplastics used on the R44 II, according to the Systems Description?
options: Only in the main rotor blades and tail rotor blades
Only in the skid gear and tailcone
In secondary cabin structure, engine cooling shrouds, ducts and fairings, and in the cabin doors
Exclusively in the primary fuselage structure
items.explanation: The GENERAL paragraph notes that fiberglass and thermoplastics are used in secondary cabin structure, engine cooling shrouds, and various ducts and fairings, and that the cabin doors are also constructed of fiberglass and thermoplastics.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: GENERAL (p.7-1)

items.question: How many right-side cowl doors provide access to the main gearbox, drive system, and engine on the R44 II?
options: Two right-side cowl doors
Three right-side cowl doors
Four right-side cowl doors
Five right-side cowl doors
items.explanation: Section 7 states that four right-side cowl doors provide access to the main gearbox, drive system, and engine.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: GENERAL (p.7-1)

items.question: What does the left-side engine cowl door provide access to, according to the Systems Description?
options: The fuel filler and fuel cap only
The engine oil filler and dipstick
The main gearbox oil filler and chip detector
The hydraulic reservoir and sight gauge
items.explanation: The GENERAL paragraph specifies that a left-side engine cowl door provides access to the engine oil filler and dip stick.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: GENERAL (p.7-1)

items.question: Where are the stainless steel firewalls located on the R44 II?
options: Behind the engine only
Forward of the engine only
Forward of and above the engine
Below the cabin floor
items.explanation: Section 7 states that stainless steel firewalls are located forward of and above the engine.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: GENERAL (p.7-1)

items.question: How many blades does the main rotor have, and how are they attached to the hub?
options: Two composite blades attached by flapping hinges
Three all-metal blades attached by coning hinges
Two all-metal blades mounted to the hub by coning hinges
Four all-metal blades mounted rigidly without hinges
items.explanation: The ROTOR SYSTEMS paragraph explains that the main rotor has two all-metal blades mounted to the hub by coning hinges.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: ROTOR SYSTEMS (p.7-2)

items.question: What is the purpose of the droop stops for the main rotor blades as described in Section 7?
options: To lock the blades for transport
To provide teeter hinge friction restraint which normally prevents rotor teetering while starting or stopping
To limit maximum rotor RPM in flight
To automatically fold the blades on shutdown
items.explanation: Section 7 notes that droop stops for the main rotor blades provide a teeter hinge friction restraint which normally prevents the rotor from teetering while starting or stopping.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: ROTOR SYSTEMS (p.7-2)

items.question: What material is used for the thick spar at the leading edge of each main rotor blade, and why is the paint finish important there?
options: Aluminum spar; paint protects against ultraviolet damage only
Titanium spar; paint prevents delamination of composite skins
Stainless steel spar; paint protects against corrosion and erosion and loss of bond at the skin-to-spar line
Steel spar; paint is only decorative and has no structural role
items.explanation: The ROTOR SYSTEMS section states that each blade has a thick stainless steel spar at the leading edge which is resistant to corrosion and erosion and that blades must be refinished if the paint erodes to bare metal at the skin-to-spar bond line.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: ROTOR SYSTEMS (p.7-2)

items.question: How many blades does the tail rotor have, and what type of hub does it use?
options: Two all-metal blades with a teetering hub and fixed coning angle
Two composite blades with an articulated hub and variable coning
Three all-metal blades with a rigid hub
Four composite blades with a fully articulated hub
items.explanation: Section 7 describes the tail rotor as having two all-metal blades and a teetering hub with a fixed coning angle.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: ROTOR SYSTEMS (p.7-2)

items.question: What component is bolted directly to the engine output shaft to begin the drive system on the R44 II?
options: A chain drive sprocket
A vee-belt sheave
A bevel gear
A direct-drive shaft coupling
items.explanation: The DRIVE SYSTEM paragraph states that a vee-belt sheave is bolted directly to the engine output shaft.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: DRIVE SYSTEM (p.7-2)

items.question: Where are flexible couplings located in the R44 II drive system, according to Section 7?
options: Only at the engine output shaft
At the main gearbox input and at each end of the long tail rotor drive shaft
Only inside the tail gearbox
Only between the tail rotor and its hub
items.explanation: Section 7 explains that flexible couplings are located at the main gearbox input and at each end of the long tail rotor drive shaft.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: DRIVE SYSTEM (p.7-2)

items.question: What type of gear set does the main gearbox contain, and how is it lubricated?
options: Dual-stage spur gear set, pressure lubricated
Single-stage spiral-bevel gear set, splash lubricated
Planetary gear set, dry running
Worm gear set, grease lubricated
items.explanation: The DRIVE SYSTEM section states that the main gearbox contains a single-stage spiral-bevel gear set which is splash lubricated.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: DRIVE SYSTEM (p.7-2)

items.question: What engine powers the R44 II, as described in the POWERPLANT paragraph of Section 7?
options: One Lycoming O-360 four-cylinder, carbureted engine
One Lycoming IO-540 six-cylinder, horizontally-opposed, air-cooled, fuel-injected engine
One turbine engine with free power turbine and FADEC
One Lycoming IO-320 four-cylinder, fuel-injected engine
items.explanation: Section 7 describes the powerplant as one Lycoming IO-540 six-cylinder, horizontally-opposed, overhead-valve, air-cooled, fuel-injected engine with a wet sump oil system.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: POWERPLANT (p.7-3)

items.question: What are pilots explicitly instructed to verify before flight in the FLIGHT CONTROLS description?
options: That they can apply full control travel in all directions
That the cyclic friction is fully tightened
That the governor switch is OFF
That the landing lights are operating
items.explanation: Section 7 FLIGHT CONTROLS states that pilots should always verify the ability to apply full control travel prior to flight.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: FLIGHT CONTROLS (p.7-4)

items.question: What technique is recommended above 6000 feet where throttle-collective correlation and governor are less effective?
options: Make rapid power changes to maintain rotor RPM tightly
Avoid using the governor and fly on manual throttle only
Make power changes slowly and smoothly
Keep collective fixed and control power only with throttle
items.explanation: A caution in the FLIGHT CONTROLS section states that above 6000 feet throttle-collective correlation and governor are less effective and that power changes should be slow and smooth.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: FLIGHT CONTROLS (p.7-4)

items.question: At high power settings above 6000 feet, how is rotor RPM typically controlled according to the FLIGHT CONTROLS section?
options: By the governor only, with throttle usually closed
By collective, because throttle is frequently wide open
By tail rotor pedals, changing rotor drag
By cyclic inputs, changing airspeed
items.explanation: The FLIGHT CONTROLS caution notes that at high power settings above 6000 feet the throttle is frequently wide open and RPM must be controlled with collective.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: FLIGHT CONTROLS (p.7-4)

items.question: How are right-side tail rotor pedals adjusted on the R44 II?
options: By turning a friction knob next to each pedal
By removing a quick-release pin, sliding the pedal to one of three positions, and reinstalling the pin
By loosening a clamp and sliding pedals along a tube with no detents
They are not adjustable
items.explanation: Section 7 FLIGHT CONTROLS explains that right-side tail rotor pedals are adjustable by removing the quick-release pin, sliding the pedal to the most comfortable of three adjustment positions, and reinstalling the pin.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: FLIGHT CONTROLS (p.7-4)

items.question: What provision does the FLIGHT CONTROLS section describe for shorter pilots using the left-side pedals?
options: A screw jack to raise and lower the pedals
Detents giving three preset pedal positions
Optional pedals that may be installed instead of standard pedals
A cable adjuster that the pilot can turn in flight
items.explanation: The FLIGHT CONTROLS section states that left-side pedals are not adjustable, but optional pedals designed for shorter pilots (Robinson part nos. F755-9 and -10) may be installed in place of standard pedals.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: FLIGHT CONTROLS (p.7-4)

items.question: According to REMOVABLE FLIGHT CONTROLS, what is the correct first step to remove the left seat cyclic grip?
options: Rotate the cyclic cross tube one full turn, then pull the grip off
Remove the quick-release pin by depressing the button and pulling, then pull outward on the left grip while supporting the cyclic center post
Loosen the knurled ring and pull the cyclic post straight up
Disconnect the balance spring before pulling the grip off
items.explanation: The REMOVABLE FLIGHT CONTROLS section instructs that to remove the cyclic grip, the quick-release pin is removed by depressing the button and pulling, then the left grip is pulled outward while supporting the cyclic center post.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: REMOVABLE FLIGHT CONTROLS (p.7-5)

items.question: What is the consequence of over-rotating the cyclic cross tube in either direction when handling the left cyclic grip?
options: It can cause hydraulic fluid loss
It will damage the balance spring
It may disconnect the governor linkage
It will bend the cyclic center post
items.explanation: A caution in the REMOVABLE FLIGHT CONTROLS section warns that overrotating the cyclic cross tube in either wound or unwound direction will damage the balance spring.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: REMOVABLE FLIGHT CONTROLS (p.7-5)

items.question: Why does the REMOVABLE FLIGHT CONTROLS section require placing a plastic cap on the exposed cyclic cross tube after removing the cyclic grip?
options: To prevent dirt from entering the cross tube
To reduce glare from bare metal
To prevent possible injury to the left seat passenger
To provide extra friction for the remaining cyclic
items.explanation: A caution states that after removing the cyclic grip, a plastic cap should be placed on the exposed cyclic cross tube to prevent possible injury to the left seat passenger.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: REMOVABLE FLIGHT CONTROLS (p.7-5)

items.question: When reinstalling the removable collective, what must be ensured according to the caution in REMOVABLE FLIGHT CONTROLS?
options: That the boot is removed to keep the locking pins visible in flight
That both locking pins are fully engaged through holes on each side
That the collective friction is fully applied
That the cyclic is held in the neutral position
items.explanation: The REMOVABLE FLIGHT CONTROLS section cautions that when the collective is installed, both locking pins must be fully engaged through holes on each side.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: REMOVABLE FLIGHT CONTROLS (p.7-5)

items.question: How is collective friction adjusted according to the CONTROL FRICTION ADJUSTMENT section?
options: By turning a knob on the center console clockwise to increase friction
By pulling the collective friction lever aft to increase friction and pushing it forward to release it
By moving a slider on the cyclic stick grip
By pressing a guarded switch on the overhead panel
items.explanation: Section 7 states that the collective friction lever is located near the aft end of the pilot’s collective and is actuated aft to increase friction and forward to release it.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: CONTROL FRICTION ADJUSTMENT (p.7-6)

items.question: Where is the cyclic friction knob located, and what happens when it is turned clockwise?
options: On the right side of the instrument console; turning clockwise reduces friction
On the left side of the cyclic center post; turning clockwise applies friction to both longitudinal and lateral cyclic
On top of the cyclic grip; turning clockwise locks the cyclic centrally
On the collective stick; turning clockwise increases throttle friction only
items.explanation: The CONTROL FRICTION ADJUSTMENT section describes the cyclic friction knob as being located left of the cyclic center post and that turning it clockwise applies friction to both longitudinal and lateral cyclic.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: CONTROL FRICTION ADJUSTMENT (p.7-6)

items.question: What caution is given about using control friction during flight?
options: Friction should always be set to maximum to prevent control backlash
Too little friction will damage control bearings
Excessive friction may make the helicopter difficult to control
Friction may only be used when hydraulics are off
items.explanation: A caution in the CONTROL FRICTION ADJUSTMENT section warns that control friction must be used with caution during flight because excessive friction may make the helicopter difficult to control.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: CONTROL FRICTION ADJUSTMENT (p.7-6)

items.question: When is the RPM governor active and how is it switched on or off?
options: Active above 60% engine RPM and controlled by a toggle switch on the instrument panel
Active above 80% engine RPM and controlled by a toggle switch on the end of the right seat collective
Active only during autorotation practice and controlled by a floor-mounted lever
Active at all RPM as soon as the master switch is on
items.explanation: The RPM GOVERNOR section states that the governor is active only above 80% engine RPM and can be switched on or off using the toggle switch on the end of the right seat collective.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: RPM GOVERNOR (p.7-6)

items.question: What limitation of the RPM governor is specifically mentioned in the POH?
options: It cannot be overridden by the pilot
It may not prevent over- or under-speed conditions generated by aggressive flight maneuvers
It must be switched off above 6000 feet density altitude
It only functions with the hydraulic system off
items.explanation: The RPM GOVERNOR section notes that the governor is designed to assist in controlling RPM under normal conditions and may not prevent over- or under-speed conditions generated by aggressive flight maneuvers.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: RPM GOVERNOR (p.7-6)

items.question: Which combination correctly describes the hydraulic system working fluid and normal operating pressure range?
options: MIL-H-5606 fluid; 150 to 200 psi
MIL-H-5606 fluid; 450 to 500 psi
Engine oil; 60 to 90 psi
Skydrol; 1200 to 1500 psi
items.explanation: The HYDRAULIC SYSTEM section states that the working fluid is MIL-H-5606 and normal operating pressure is 450 to 500 psi.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: HYDRAULIC SYSTEM (p.7-7)

items.question: Which components make up the R44 II hydraulic system according to the Systems Description?
options: A pump, three servos, a reservoir, and interconnecting lines
Two pumps, one servo, and a hydraulic accumulator only
A pump, a single servo, and the main rotor gearbox only
An electric pump, accumulator, and tail rotor servo only
items.explanation: The HYDRAULIC SYSTEM paragraph states that the hydraulic system consists of a pump, three servos, a reservoir, and interconnecting lines.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: HYDRAULIC SYSTEM (p.7-7)

items.question: Where is the hydraulic pump mounted and how is it driven?
options: On the engine accessory case and driven by the engine crankshaft
On the main gearbox and driven by the main gearbox
On the tail rotor gearbox and driven by the tail rotor shaft
Under the cabin floor and driven by an electric motor
items.explanation: Section 7 explains that the hydraulic pump is mounted on and driven by the main gearbox.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: HYDRAULIC SYSTEM (p.7-7)

items.question: How is the hydraulic reservoir described with respect to location and features?
options: It is under the left front seat and checked with a dipstick only

It is mounted on the steel tube frame behind the main gearbox and includes a filter, pressure relief valve, pilot-controlled pressure shut-off valve, and a sight gage visible through a right side cowl door
It is located in the nose and incorporates only a sight gage and vent
It is attached directly to the pump and has no external level indication
items.explanation: The HYDRAULIC SYSTEM section notes that the reservoir is mounted on the steel tube frame behind the main gearbox, includes a filter, pressure relief valve, and pilot-controlled pressure shut-off valve, and has a sight gage visible by opening a right side cowl door.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: HYDRAULIC SYSTEM (p.7-7)

items.question: What does the hydraulic switch on the pilot's cyclic control, and how should it normally be set during shutdown and start up?
options: It directly vents hydraulic pressure to the reservoir and should normally be OFF during shutdown and start up
It controls a solenoid-actuated pressure shut-off valve and should normally be left ON during shutdown and start up except during the hydraulic system check
It turns the hydraulic pump on and off mechanically and should be cycled several times during start up
It only illuminates the HYD caution light and has no effect on system pressure
items.explanation: Section 7 states that the pressure shut-off valve is solenoid-actuated and controlled by the hydraulic switch on the pilot's cyclic, and that the switch should be left ON during helicopter shutdown and start up except during the hydraulic system check.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: HYDRAULIC SYSTEM (p.7-7)

items.question: What is the effect of pulling the HYD circuit breaker according to the HYDRAULIC SYSTEM note?
options: It immediately removes hydraulic pressure and restores normal unboosted control forces
It does not turn off hydraulics but disables the hydraulic switch
It locks the servos in place and prevents any further control movement
It dumps hydraulic pressure and turns the HYD caution light off
items.explanation: The HYDRAULIC SYSTEM note specifies that electrical power is required to switch hydraulics OFF and that pulling the HYD circuit breaker will NOT turn off hydraulics but will disable the hydraulic switch.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: HYDRAULIC SYSTEM (p.7-7)

items.question: What handling characteristics are described for flight without hydraulic pressure?
options: Controls remain light but are delayed due to servo bypass valves
A large pilot input force is required to increase collective and collective inputs cause longitudinal cyclic forces, making a steady hover difficult
Collective forces decrease but cyclic forces increase, making cruise flight unstable
Control feel is unchanged because of the irreversible feature in the servos
items.explanation: Section 7 explains that without hydraulic pressure, a large pilot input force is required to increase collective and that collective inputs cause longitudinal cyclic forces, making it difficult to maintain a steady hover.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: HYDRAULIC SYSTEM (p.7-7)

items.question: What is the purpose of the irreversible feature in the main rotor servos?
options: To allow rotor feedback forces to move the controls for better feel
To prevent rotor feedback forces from moving the controls and allow the pilot to relax pressure in steady cruise, while requiring periodic collective increases after cyclic inputs
To automatically trim the helicopter in hover
To reduce hydraulic pressure at high airspeeds
items.explanation: The HYDRAULIC SYSTEM section states that the servos have an irreversible feature to prevent rotor feedback forces from moving the controls, allowing the pilot to relax pressure on the controls in steady cruise flight; however, any cyclic input will cause the collective to lower and therefore the collective must be increased periodically.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: HYDRAULIC SYSTEM (p.7-7)

items.question: Where are the twist-grip throttle controls located, and how do they actuate the throttle valve?
options: On the cyclic stick only, operating an electric throttle motor
On each collective stick, interconnected and actuating the throttle valve through a mechanical linkage
On the instrument console, controlling fuel flow electronically
On the tail rotor pedals, linked to the engine governor
items.explanation: The ENGINE CONTROLS paragraph specifies that a twist-grip throttle control is located on each collective stick, that the controls are interconnected, and that they actuate the throttle valve through a mechanical linkage.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: ENGINE CONTROLS (p.7-8)

items.question: Under which conditions is manual manipulation of the twist-grip throttle typically required?
options: Only during cruise when changing altitude
Only during takeoff and landing
During start up, shut down, autorotation practice, and emergencies
Only during high-density-altitude operations
items.explanation: Section 7 ENGINE CONTROLS states that manual manipulation of the twist-grip is not typically required except during start up, shut down, autorotation practice, and emergencies.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: ENGINE CONTROLS (p.7-8)

items.question: What is the purpose of the overtravel spring in the throttle linkage?
options: To assist the governor in opening the throttle during rapid power changes
To allow the pilot to roll the throttle off beyond the idle stop before a ground contact autorotation landing so the throttle does not open when collective is raised
To provide automatic throttle closure at low RPM
To prevent the throttle from ever reaching the full-open position
items.explanation: The ENGINE CONTROLS section explains that an overtravel spring in the throttle linkage allows the pilot to roll the throttle off beyond the idle stop prior to a ground contact (run-on) autorotation landing, preventing the throttle from opening when the collective is raised.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: ENGINE CONTROLS (p.7-8)

items.question: Where is the fuel shutoff valve control located and what does it control?
options: On the overhead panel; it controls only the auxiliary tank
Between the front seats; it controls flow from both main and auxiliary tanks to the engine
On the left cabin sidewall; it controls only the main tank
On the cyclic center post; it shuts off fuel only to the fuel control
items.explanation: The FUEL SYSTEM section states that the system includes main and auxiliary tanks and a shutoff valve control located between the front seats, and that the fuel shutoff valve controls flow from both tanks to the engine.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: FUEL SYSTEM (p.7-10–7-11)

items.question: How does the auxiliary (electric) fuel pump normally operate and what is indicated when the clutch switch is disengaged?
options: It only runs during start; with the clutch disengaged the AUX FUEL PUMP light should be off

It primes the engine for starting and then runs continuously in flight to provide redundancy; when the clutch switch is disengaged the auxiliary pump is off and the AUX FUEL PUMP caution light should be illuminated
It runs only above 60 KIAS and the AUX FUEL PUMP light should always be out in flight
It is used only for crossfeed and has no associated caution light
items.explanation: Section 7 FUEL SYSTEM explains that the auxiliary pump primes the engine for starting and then runs in flight to provide fuel pump redundancy, and that when the clutch switch is disengaged the auxiliary pump is off and the AUX FUEL PUMP caution light should be illuminated.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: FUEL SYSTEM (p.7-10)

items.question: What preflight fuel sampling procedure is described for the gascolator and tank sumps?
options: Sample only the main tank sump if contamination is suspected
Sample only after maintenance, using the fuel cap opening

Use the plunger-style drain valves at the gascolator and each fuel tank sump, extending the plastic tubes and pushing on the plungers, and sample from all three locations prior to the first flight of the day and after refueling
Drain the main tank completely at the end of each day
items.explanation: The FUEL SYSTEM (cont'd) section describes plunger-style drain valves for the gascolator and each fuel tank sump, explains how to drain them using the plastic tubes, and states that fuel should be sampled from all three locations prior to the first flight of the day and after refueling.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: FUEL SYSTEM (p.7-11)

items.question: In flight, what does an ALT caution light or a discharge indication on the ammeter signify, and what is the recommended initial action?
options: High voltage; immediately switch the alternator off and leave it off for the remainder of the flight
Low voltage and possible alternator failure; turn off nonessential electrical equipment and switch the alternator off then back on after one second to reset the alternator control unit
Battery over-temperature; turn the battery switch off and continue flight
Normal battery charging; no action is required
items.explanation: The ELECTRICAL SYSTEM section states that an ALT caution light or ammeter discharge indication in flight indicates low voltage and possible alternator failure, and recommends turning off nonessential electrical equipment and switching the alternator off then back on after one second to reset the alternator control unit.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: ELECTRICAL SYSTEM (p.7-12)

items.question: Why does the ELECTRICAL SYSTEM section advise against operating the alternator with the battery switched off during normal operations?
options: Because the alternator will not produce power without the battery
Because the battery helps protect electrical equipment from voltage spikes
Because the tachometers will not function with the battery on
Because the alternator cooling fan is driven only when the battery is on
items.explanation: The ELECTRICAL SYSTEM section notes that, except for emergency procedures, the alternator should not be operated with the battery switched off because the battery helps protect electrical equipment from voltage spikes.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: ELECTRICAL SYSTEM (p.7-12)

items.question: Where is the red anti-collision light located and which switch controls it?
options: On the nose, controlled by the nav lights switch
On the tailcone, controlled by the strobe switch
On each side of the cabin, controlled by the battery switch
On top of the mast fairing, controlled by the clutch switch
items.explanation: The LIGHTING SYSTEM section states that a red anti-collision light is installed on the tailcone and is controlled by the strobe switch.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: LIGHTING SYSTEM (p.7-17)

items.question: Which statement correctly describes the landing lights on the R44 II?
options: A single landing light in the nose is controlled by a switch on the overhead panel and operates whenever the battery switch is on
Two landing lights in the nose are controlled by one switch on the cyclic center post and operate only when the clutch actuator switch is in the ENGAGE position
Two landing lights are mounted on the skid gear and operate automatically whenever engine RPM exceeds 80%
A single landing light is mounted on the tailcone and operates only when the nav lights switch is on
items.explanation: Section 7 LIGHTING SYSTEM explains that two landing lights are installed in the nose at different vertical angles, are controlled by one landing light switch on the cyclic center post, and operate only when the clutch actuator switch is in the engage position.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: LIGHTING SYSTEM (p.7-17)

items.question: How are instrument and map lights operated according to the LIGHTING SYSTEM description?
options: Instrument lights operate whenever the battery switch is on; the map light is tied to the alternator switch

Instrument lighting is active when the nav lights switch is on and is dimmed by a knob above the nav lights switch; an overhead map light on a swivel is controlled by an adjacent switch and may be used for emergency lighting of the instrument panel
Instrument lighting is controlled solely by a rheostat on the cyclic center post; the map light operates automatically at night
Instrument and map lights are both controlled by the strobe switch
items.explanation: The LIGHTING SYSTEM paragraph states that instrument lighting is active when the nav lights switch is on and dimmed via the knob above the nav lights switch, and that an overhead map light on a swivel is controlled by an adjacent switch and may be used for emergency lighting of the instrument panel.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: LIGHTING SYSTEM (p.7-17)

items.question: What do the ICS volume and VOX squelch knobs control on the standard audio panel?
options: The ICS volume knob controls both intercom and radio volume; the VOX knob controls radio squelch only

The ICS volume knob controls intercom volume but not radio volume; the VOX knob sets the threshold at which the intercom is activated and when turned fully clockwise keying is required to activate the intercom
The ICS volume knob controls only radio volume; the VOX knob mutes the intercom entirely
The ICS volume knob adjusts headset sidetone; the VOX knob controls marker beacon audio
items.explanation: The AUDIO SYSTEM section explains that the ICS volume knob controls intercom volume but does not affect radio volume, and that the VOX squelch knob sets the threshold volume at which the intercom is activated; when turned fully clockwise, keying is required to activate the intercom.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: AUDIO SYSTEM (p.7-23)

items.question: What is the function of the PILOT ISO mode on the audio control panel?
options: It disconnects all headsets from the intercom and radios
It connects the pilot only to the intercom while everyone else hears the radios
It connects the pilot only to the radio while the copilot and rear passengers remain connected to each other via the intercom
It mutes all audio alerts but leaves radio audio on
items.explanation: The AUDIO SYSTEM description states that a toggle switch allows selection of PILOT ISO mode in which the pilot is connected only to the radio while the copilot and rear passengers remain connected to each other via the intercom.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: AUDIO SYSTEM (p.7-23)

items.question: Which instruments are driven by the pitot-static system and where are the pitot and static sources located?
options: Only the altimeter; pitot tube on the tailcone and static ports in the nose
The airspeed indicator and altimeter only; pitot tube on the nose and static ports under the cabin floor
The airspeed indicator, altimeter, and vertical speed indicator; pitot tube on the front edge of the mast fairing and static sources on each side of the cabin aft of the rear doors
Only the vertical speed indicator; pitot tube on the mast and static ports in the tail rotor pylon
items.explanation: The PITOT-STATIC SYSTEM section states that the system supplies air pressure to the airspeed indicator, altimeter, and vertical speed indicator, that the pitot tube is located on the front edge of the mast fairing, and that the static sources are on each side of the cabin aft of the rear doors.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: PITOT-STATIC SYSTEM (p.7-24)

items.question: When should the pitot-static lines be drained according to the PITOT-STATIC SYSTEM description?
options: At the end of every flight regardless of indication
Only after flying in rain or visible moisture
Only when the airspeed indicator or altimeter appears erratic, by removing the plastic drain plugs accessible through the forward inspection panel on the cabin underside
Whenever the helicopter is parked outside overnight
items.explanation: Section 7 notes that water can be drained from the pitot-static lines by removing the plastic drain plugs accessible through the forward inspection panel on the underside of the cabin, and that draining should be required only if the airspeed indicator or altimeter appears erratic.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: PITOT-STATIC SYSTEM (p.7-24)

items.question: Why should the helicopter not be stowed with the clutch actuator switch in the ENGAGE position, according to the DUAL TACHOMETER note?
options: Because the clutch actuator will overheat if left engaged
Because the tachometers remain powered through a bypass circuit when the clutch is engaged and will discharge the battery
Because the main gearbox chip detectors are powered only with the clutch engaged
Because the governor cannot complete its self-test unless the clutch is disengaged
items.explanation: The DUAL TACHOMETER section explains that with the battery and alternator switches off, the tachometers continue to receive power from the battery through a bypass circuit as long as the clutch actuator switch is in the engage position, and the note specifically warns not to stow the helicopter with the clutch switch engaged because the tachometers will discharge the battery.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: DUAL TACHOMETER (p.7-24)

items.question: When do the LOW RPM light and horn activate, and how can the horn be muted?
options: They activate when rotor RPM exceeds 108%; the horn can be muted by switching the governor off
They activate when driveline speed is below 97% RPM; the horn is muted when the collective is fully down
They activate whenever engine RPM drops below 80%; the horn can be muted by pulling the circuit breaker
They activate only on the ground during run-up; the horn is automatically muted in flight
items.explanation: The WARNING AND CAUTION LIGHTS section states that the LOW RPM light and horn are activated by a sensor at the aft end of the main gearbox when driveline speed is below 97% RPM, and the AUDIO ALERTS section notes that the horn is muted when the collective is fully down.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: WARNING AND CAUTION LIGHTS & AUDIO ALERTS (p.7-25–7-26)

items.question: What should occur when the annunciator panel test button is pressed on aircraft equipped with an annunciator panel?
options: Only the LOW FUEL and LOW RPM segments should illuminate
All annunciator segments and the FULL THROTTLE and BRAKE lights should illuminate while the button is depressed
Only the EMU segment should illuminate after a ten-second delay
Only the HYD and EMU segments should illuminate and remain on after the button is released
items.explanation: The WARNING AND CAUTION LIGHTS (cont'd) section states that the annunciator panel includes a test button which should cause all panel segments, as well as the FULL THROTTLE and BRAKE lights, to illuminate when depressed.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: WARNING AND CAUTION LIGHTS (p.7-26)

items.question: What do the HYD and EMU segments on the annunciator panel indicate?
options: HYD indicates hydraulic pressure is high; EMU illuminates whenever the alternator fails
HYD illuminates when the hydraulic system is switched off; EMU indicates Engine Monitoring Unit status and will illuminate only when the test button is depressed after the EMU completes its self-test
HYD indicates the hydraulic reservoir is low; EMU comes on whenever the governor is off
HYD and EMU are used only for ground maintenance and never illuminate in flight
items.explanation: Section 7 explains that aircraft with annunciator panels include HYD and EMU segments, that the HYD segment illuminates when the hydraulic system is switched off, and that the EMU segment indicates Engine Monitoring Unit status and will illuminate only when the annunciator test button is depressed after the EMU completes its self-test.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: WARNING AND CAUTION LIGHTS & ENGINE MONITORING UNIT (p.7-26–7-27)

items.question: In case of an in-flight engine fire, what action regarding cabin heat is recommended and why?
options: Turn cabin heat full on to keep the windshield clear
Leave cabin heat as set to avoid disturbing airflow
Turn cabin heat off to seal the cabin area from the engine compartment
Cycle cabin heat on and off to check for fumes
items.explanation: The CABIN HEATING AND VENTILATION section cautions that in case of an in-flight engine fire, cabin heat should be turned off to seal the cabin area from the engine compartment.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: CABIN HEATING AND VENTILATION (p.7-28)

items.question: According to the LANDING GEAR description, when must a landing gear crosstube be replaced after a hard landing?
options: Any time there is any visible bending of the crosstube
Whenever the tail skid touches the ground during landing
When yielding allows the tail skid to be within 30 inches of the ground with the helicopter sitting empty on level pavement
Only when a skid fairing is damaged
items.explanation: The LANDING GEAR section states that slight crosstube yielding is acceptable, but yielding which allows the tail skid to be within 30 inches of the ground when the helicopter is sitting empty on level pavement requires crosstube replacement.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: LANDING GEAR (p.7-29)

items.question: Which rotor brake operating technique is recommended to avoid damage to the brake shoes?
options: Apply the rotor brake immediately when mixture is pulled off and stop the rotor as quickly as possible
Wait at least 30 seconds after the engine stops before applying the brake, use moderate force, and avoid stopping the rotor in less than 20 seconds
Apply maximum force to stop the rotor within 10 seconds whenever possible
Use the rotor brake only in flight to control rotor RPM
items.explanation: The ROTOR BRAKE section states that the brake should be applied using moderate force after pulling mixture off and waiting at least 30 seconds, and the caution warns that applying the brake without waiting at least 30 seconds after engine stop or using a force which stops the rotor in less than 20 seconds may damage the brake shoes.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: ROTOR BRAKE (p.7-30)

items.question: What actions are recommended if the carbon monoxide (CO) caution light illuminates and symptoms of CO poisoning are present?
options: Ignore the light if engine instruments are normal and continue flight
Open only the rear door vents and continue hovering to clear the fumes

Shut off the heater, open nose and door vents as required to ventilate the cabin, land or transition to forward flight, and if symptoms such as headache or drowsiness accompany the light, land immediately and have the exhaust system inspected before the next flight
Switch the battery off and close all vents to prevent more CO from entering
items.explanation: The CARBON MONOXIDE DETECTOR section instructs that if the caution light illuminates, the heater should be shut off and the nose and door vents opened as required to ventilate the cabin, that if hovering the pilot should land or transition to forward flight, and that if symptoms of CO poisoning accompany the caution light, the helicopter should be landed immediately and the exhaust system inspected before the next flight.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: CARBON MONOXIDE DETECTOR (p.7-31)

items.question: What ADS-B capability is installed on later R44 II aircraft and what is its primary regulatory purpose?
options: ADS-B In only, required to display traffic on cockpit screens
ADS-B Out capability, required for operation in certain airspace and to transmit GPS position to ATC
ADS-B In and Out, required only for international flights
ADS-B In only, required for weather reception
items.explanation: The ADS-B EQUIPMENT section explains that an ADS-B capable transponder is installed on later aircraft, that ADS-B Out operation is required in certain airspace, and that the transponder transmits GPS position information to air traffic control to supplement radar/transponder information.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: ADS-B EQUIPMENT (p.7-32)

items.question: What frequency does factory-installed ADS-B Out equipment use, and what advisory is given about selecting ADS-B Out off?
options: 978 MHz only; ADS-B Out should be selected off whenever flying outside the United States
1090 MHz; ADS-B Out should not be selected off unless directed by air traffic control, because it is required in certain airspace
Both 978 and 1090 MHz; ADS-B Out may be selected off at the pilot's discretion
1090 MHz; ADS-B Out must always be selected off on the ground
items.explanation: The ADS-B EQUIPMENT description states that ADS-B Out equipment installed at the factory operates on 1090 MHz and that ADS-B Out is required in certain airspace, so it should not be selected off unless directed by air traffic control.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: ADS-B EQUIPMENT (p.7-32)

items.question: What additional information can factory-installed ADS-B In equipment provide besides traffic, assuming suitable displays are installed?
options: Only terrain warnings
Only GPS position history
Traffic and, depending on equipment and country, additional traffic and weather information from ground stations
Engine performance data and maintenance alerts
items.explanation: Section 7 notes that ADS-B In equipment may receive traffic information from other ADS-B equipped aircraft and, depending on specific equipment and country, additional traffic and weather information from ground stations, when used with a suitable display such as a GPS or MFD.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: ADS-B EQUIPMENT (p.7-32)

items.question: Where is the Emergency Locator Transmitter (ELT) installed and how is it normally armed for flight?
options: Under the pilot seat with a switch that is left OFF for flight
On the tailcone with a switch that must be turned ON before each flight
On the upper steel tube frame, accessible through the aft upper cowl door, with both the transmitter switch and remote switch/annunciator secured in AUTO/ARM for flight
Inside the instrument console and armed automatically whenever the battery switch is on
items.explanation: The EMERGENCY LOCATOR TRANSMITTER section states that the transmitter is mounted to the upper steel tube frame and accessible through the aft upper cowl door, and that both the transmitter switch and the remote switch/annunciator should be in the AUTO or ARM position for flight.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: EMERGENCY LOCATOR TRANSMITTER (p.7-33)

items.question: When should the pilot move the ELT remote switch to ON, and what happens when this is done?
options: At every engine start to test the unit; no actual transmission is sent
Only when search and rescue operations are complete; the unit turns itself off
When a forced landing is imminent and time permits; the transmitter is activated, begins transmitting, and the red indicator illuminates
Only during routine maintenance tests; the transmitter enters a test mode without transmitting
items.explanation: The EMERGENCY LOCATOR TRANSMITTER section states that moving the remote switch to ON activates the transmitter and that this may be used if a forced landing is imminent and time permits. When the transmitter is operating, the red indicator light is illuminated.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: EMERGENCY LOCATOR TRANSMITTER (p.7-33)

items.question: What is the recommended action if the ELT is activated inadvertently?
options: Allow it to continue transmitting until the battery is discharged
Turn the helicopter battery switch off to stop the transmission
Use the RESET position on the remote switch to stop the transmission and reset the unit so that the red indicator extinguishes
Remove the ELT from the helicopter as soon as possible
items.explanation: The EMERGENCY LOCATOR TRANSMITTER description explains that if the ELT is activated inadvertently, the pilot should place the remote switch to RESET to stop the transmission and reset the unit. The red indicator light will extinguish when the unit is reset.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: EMERGENCY LOCATOR TRANSMITTER (p.7-33)

items.question: What is the purpose of the optional accessory mounts located in front of the pilot and/or copilot?
options: To provide additional structure for hard landings
To provide approved mounting locations for small portable equipment such as tablets using compatible clamps and power outlets
To serve as handholds for emergency egress only
To support auxiliary fuel tanks
items.explanation: The ACCESSORY MOUNTS section describes bars installed in front of the pilot and/or copilot with clamp mechanisms compatible with several commercially available mounting brackets and with power outlets. They are intended as secure mounting locations for small portable items such as electronic devices.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: ACCESSORY MOUNTS (p.7-34)

items.question: What is the total weight limit per accessory bar, and what is its practical implication for the pilot?
options: 5 lb; only one small device may be mounted
10 lb; the pilot must ensure that the total weight of all items attached to each bar does not exceed 10 lb and that they do not interfere with controls or visibility
25 lb; there are no practical restrictions
No specific limit; any equipment is allowed as long as it is secured
items.explanation: The ACCESSORY MOUNTS description sets a 10 lb total weight limit for items attached to each bar and emphasizes that mounted equipment must not interfere with flight controls or primary visibility.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: ACCESSORY MOUNTS (p.7-34)

items.question: How are recordings to the cockpit camera's flash memory started and stopped when the helicopter battery switch is ON?
options: Recording to flash starts and stops automatically with rotor RPM and cannot be controlled manually

Recording starts automatically when the helicopter battery switch is turned on and stops when it is turned off; recording to flash can be stopped manually with the record switch on the camera housing before removing the memory card
Recording must always be started and stopped manually with the record switch regardless of the battery switch
Recording occurs only when a separate cockpit-camera switch is ON
items.explanation: The COCKPIT CAMERA section states that the camera begins recording when the helicopter battery switch is turned on and stops when the battery switch is turned off, and that recording to flash memory may be stopped using the record switch before the memory card is removed.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: COCKPIT CAMERA (p.7-35)

items.question: What is the consequence of removing the flash memory card while a recording is in progress according to the cockpit camera description?
options: None; files are closed automatically
Only the last file is deleted but all previous files remain intact
The video file that is being recorded will be corrupted
The camera enters a test mode
items.explanation: The COCKPIT CAMERA section warns that the flash memory card must not be removed while a recording is in progress because the video file being recorded will be corrupted.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: COCKPIT CAMERA (p.7-35)

items.question: What division of responsibility is described for use of the accessory mounts and cockpit camera with respect to the type certificate?
options: All equipment attached to the mounts is covered by the type certificate and requires no pilot discretion
Only the camera is part of the type certificate; all other items are prohibited

The mounting bars, clamps, power outlets, and camera installation are part of the type certificate, but whatever the pilot attaches to the bars and chooses to record is the pilot in command's responsibility under applicable operating rules
All use of accessories must be approved by maintenance personnel before each flight
items.explanation: The ACCESSORY MOUNTS and COCKPIT CAMERA sections emphasize that the mounts, clamps, power outlets, and camera are part of the type design, but that the equipment attached to the bars and how it is used are the pilot in command's responsibility under the relevant operating rules.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: ACCESSORY MOUNTS & COCKPIT CAMERA (p.7-34–7-36)

items.question: What is the primary purpose of the optional cyclic guard?
options: To act as a structural brace between the seat and console
To serve as an armrest for the pilot
To act as a barrier that helps prevent inadvertent contact with the cyclic control while also providing a handhold for the passenger's right hand
To lock the cyclic in the neutral position on the ground
items.explanation: The CYCLIC GUARD section explains that the bar is intended to act as a barrier to help prevent inadvertent interference with the cyclic control and also to provide a handhold for the passenger's right hand.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: CYCLIC GUARD (p.7-36)

items.question: What must be done with the cyclic guard to access the under-seat compartment, and what is the recommended use when a non-pilot occupies the left front seat?
options: Remove two screws and take the guard off completely; the guard should always be removed when someone sits in the left seat
Pull the spring-loaded knob at the front so the rear portion can be rotated down, and it is recommended that the guard be installed when a non-pilot occupies the left front seat
Slide the guard forward and up; it should be used only when the pilot sits in the left seat
Flex the guard to the side to open the seat; the guard should never be used with passengers
items.explanation: The CYCLIC GUARD section states that to access the compartment under the seat, the spring-loaded knob at the front of the guard is pulled and the rear portion is rotated down, and it recommends that the guard be installed when a non-pilot is seated in the left front seat.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: CYCLIC GUARD (p.7-36)

items.question: What is a potential disadvantage of the cyclic guard when the pilot is flying from the left seat?
options: It blocks access to the mixture control
It may contact the pilot's right leg when the feet are on the pedals, and should be removed before flight if the pilot finds this objectionable
It makes it difficult to reach the main switches on the instrument panel
It makes it impossible to use the left pedal
items.explanation: The CYCLIC GUARD description notes that pilots flying from the left seat may find that the guard contacts the right leg when the feet are on the pedals and recommends removing the guard before flight if the pilot finds this objectionable.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: CYCLIC GUARD (p.7-36)

items.question: What is the recommended practice for becoming familiar with installed avionics and ADS-B/EMU systems before flight?
options: Reading only the checklist is sufficient

Pilots should use manufacturer manuals and any handbook supplements; they should become familiar with the layout, installed equipment, and functions such as ADS-B, EMU, and any PFD/MFD before flying the specific aircraft
It is enough to ask the previous pilot how the systems work
No specific familiarization is required beyond the type rating
items.explanation: Several Systems Description sections, particularly those describing the instrument panel, ADS-B equipment, and the Engine Monitoring Unit, emphasize that pilots should use manufacturer manuals and relevant supplements to become familiar with the installed avionics and that they should be comfortable with how the systems operate before flying the specific aircraft.
references: R44 II POH Sec 7: INSTRUMENT PANEL, ADS-B EQUIPMENT & ENGINE MONITORING UNIT
